utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Madam Registrar, and good morning everybody. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecution versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, ma'am. For the record, all the accused are here. From the Defence teams I notice the absence of Ms. Condon, Mr. Meek, Mr. Josse, and Mr. Haynes. Prosecution, we have Mr. McCloskey, Mr. Nicholls, Ms. Soljan, no one else. So let me start from here. There is a Prosecution motion for leave to amend the 65 ter exhibit list with five expert reports. At least - not at least - one of the expert witnesses, to my knowledge, is due to start testifying soon after the current -- the witness that we'll be having today. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's -- the next witness is Kate Barr, Your Honour. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. So you will understand that we can't wait the usual time limit provided by the rules to run to have a response. If you are in a position to give us a response, your response now, I think it will be the best thing. If not, we would like to have a response, at least as far as Kathryn Barr is concerned, by the end of today's sitting so that we'll be in a position to decide the issue, but I will ask first whether you are in a position to give us a response -- your response now. We're talking of the 65 ter motion of the Prosecution filed last Friday. Yes, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. I'm not prepared to respond to the balance, with the exception of Ms. Barr. The only thing with Ms. Barr I would request is that the Prosecution produce to use the entire file which contains her analysis within the report that she's actually -- she's generated, I think five reports so we need to know the basis upon which she made her analysis. And specifically, since it's a handwriting expert, I'd like to see the chart that she created which showed which documents, and specifically which words she looked at in the duty officer log and the unofficial notebook, and made this comparison between similarities, and what they call dissimilarities or differences, in handwriting styles. So if they can produce that by the next break, I think we'll be able to proceed with at least Ms. Barr this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Ostojic. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. All the material that was used that we have has been -- have been provided, and so I'm not sure exactly what Mr. Ostojic is asking for, but if there are -- if there's anything else that she has, that she's used we will gladly provide that, but we have provided what we have, as far as I know, and these reports have been around for a long time. They're 94 bis reports and so we'll gladly provide counsel with things, but she's due to testify any minute, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. To be more specific, for example, this morning we were tendered two pages, I think from the Prosecution, was sitting on our desk which has one page with the questioned specimen as they call it, and then the next questioned writing, and the next page, which is the second page which is the specimen writing, which is supposedly from one of the individuals that the report was generated against or for. We don't have that for the entire process that Ms. Barr was engaged in or involved in. With -- these two pages are obviously limited. Her report considers a complete overview of the entire Zvornik Brigade logbook and the unofficial notebook that we do have, that we expect to question her on however I don't have her specimens, specifically the question and the specimen that she pulled out to show us how she made this comparative analysis that she did. So this was handed to us this morning on our desk and we didn't have it other than this morning but I'm sure that there's more, and this is what experts rely on and they look at each specific word to make correlations or comparisons to person's handwriting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can't this be elaborated in the course of the examination-in-chief and the cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It could, I guess. It may take a little longer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I mean, in each case that I have been involved here there has always been handwriting experts and most of the time these questions have arisen obviously, but they arise in either the course of the examination-in-chief or the cross-examination, and sometimes you find that the expert witness has the necessary documents in his or her briefcase, which then come out. I don't know, because obviously I haven't gone into her report or whatever because --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, neither do we. All we're asking for, Your Honour, with all due respect, is that we be given that. And we can handle it just if we give it during her testimony. If they want to give it to us late, that's, I guess, not acceptable, but we'll have to live with it. But giving it to us piecemeal is not acceptable to me and I think there's other specimens that they can provide to us, but we can proceed with her if that's what the Court desires.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, the two documents that were provided were the documents that Ms. Barr used in the Blagojevic trial and are referred to in the testimony and it was used as an example for her testimony to illustrate what she did. I don't believe she did -- it's the only example that we have. What she keeps -- I don't know if she keeps anything else, but these were the publicly used documents before and so there's -- there's no mystery to them. But if there is material, we'll gladly try to get whatever we can for the accused but this is what we know of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's go -- yes, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And then I'll give you the floor Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just want to correct the record from what Mr. McCloskey says. That's just not an accurate statement. They have listed in their 65 ter list other sample specimens of questioned writing and specimen writings. To suggest that these are the only two is not accurate. What I'm requesting is that we get the complete file. They have given us some for one report, they have given us some this morning that was not provided to us earlier, and there's obviously others based on her report. So to suggest that she only has these two -- they've listed in their prior 65 ter list, we have those specimen copies, I still believe that it's inadequate but just to make the record clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: These are not specimen copies. What we provided was what she used as an exhibit to help show the court her comparison of the Jokic handwriting last time. Of the specimen copies, meaning old writing from various people have been provided to the Defence for a long time as far as I know, but again, we haven't had a -- we haven't -- this is the first time the Defence has really talked to us about this and we'll get together with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. This is just to say that we received from the Prosecution a list of Prosecution exhibits for this witness in order to allow us to, of course, prepare. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Will you look into that, Mr. McCloskey, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, of course, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And perhaps you can deal with it tete-a-tete during the first break.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Let's go into private session for a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session. Any preliminaries? Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know, I'm trying to recall if there are exhibits we needed to deal with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is not preliminary. That would be part of the agenda. I'm coming to that. No preliminaries. So the next matter that we need to deal with is the exhibits tendered with the evidence of Mr. Acimovic. Do you have any exhibits, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I used 65 ter number 295 with him but that has been previously admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, and Mr. Bourgon in particular. Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We'll not have anything else but also 295, same exhibit tendered by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Mr. Bourgon. Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: We do have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Mr. Zivanovic, are you not tendering 312?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry. Sorry. We ask to tender Exhibit 312 through 808, and 295.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have one. Okay. All right. Sorry, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: For the record, I don't think this is 312 through 801, but they are the identical exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It was marked -- 312. All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objections on the part of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: On the part of any of the other Defence teams? So this is admitted. Mr. Bourgon, again my apologies to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good morning again, Mr. President. Just one document that we would like to tender - and if my colleague consents, I did not approach him yet - and that's the Drinski magazine article, The Unbreakables or The Untouchables, I don't know which one it was again, but if my colleague consents to that. Because I did discuss it with the witness without ever showing it to him for the sake of expediency.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No objection. Does it have --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: That is, 3D has a translation, and it's on 3D171 [Realtime transcript read in error "3D1171"].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. Bourgon. Any objection by anyone? No objection so it's standard and admitted. All right. Can we proceed with the next witness? No protective measures for this witness, no?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Good morning to you, ma'am. Yes, Mr. Bourgon. It's -- I don't know if you are surprised.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Quick correction, Mr. President. Just on -- at line -- page 8, line 6 should read 3D171 and not 1171. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you for that correction, Mr. Bourgon. Madam Registrar, please take note of that. What happened to Mitar Lazarevic? That's why I asked whether there were protective measures. I was under the impression that --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That was the witness today.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, Lazarevic and Milosevic are here. However, Ms. Barr is -- is an expert from the UK, had a schedule that we had been planning on having her this Monday and we've been -- there's been several e-mails about that and it got slightly confused and I believe the Court was in on those e-mails which may have confused it even more, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: My Senior Legal Officer this morning did tell me that Ms. Barr is the next witness, but I imagined he meant after Lazarevic. So in my mind, it was still Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We are not informed that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have been informed, in other words. I take it that you were -- yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was not. I was not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I wasn't from that. And in fact, for a moment I was is surprised because I thought that Mitar is not the name of a -- of a man but the name of a woman.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I apologise about this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's okay, it's okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- confusion I know the word went out to Mr. Cubbon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah, Mr. Cubbon did tell me this morning. But I understood that to mean after Lazarevic. So it's okay, you have no problems with procedure. Yes, Madam Bourgon. Madam Fauveau. Well, you are exchanging opinions all the time, so that's why -- that's why the confusion. Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to inform the Chamber that in fact we were informed but only on Friday evening and there was an exchange of messages between the OTP and the Defence because it was total confusion amongst us as well. Until last evening I was not at all certain which witness we are going to hear today. So I would like to ask you to ask the Prosecutor to give us more notice in the future. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Mr. McCloskey, you've heard that. Ms. Barr, good morning, to you, and welcome to this Tribunal. You're about to start giving evidence. It's not your first time here, so you know what the procedure is. Madam Usher is going to hand you the text of the solemn declaration that our rules require. Please let's proceed with that and that's your solemn undertaking with us, that you'll be testifying the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Please make yourself comfortable. Yes, Ms. Soljan will go first for the Prosecution, and she will then be followed by the Defence teams on cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Barr. Could you please begin by telling the Trial Chamber your full name?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: Yes, Kathryn Jean Barr.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And what is your educational background for us briefly?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: I've got a Bachelor of Arts and a Master of Arts and I'm also -- I've got a Ph.D.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And your Ph.D. is in what precise area?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: Plant pathology.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: What is your first job upon receiving your Ph.D.?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: I became a forensic documents examiner.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And when was this?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And what kind of work did a forensic document examiner do or does a forensic document examiner do?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: Most of the work that we do involves using handwriting and signatures as a means of identification of specific person, or grouping documents as having been written by one person. We also do other examinations involving documents, for example, typewriting, printers, counterfeit documents, indented impressions, alterations, obliterations.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And in order to become proficient in the work that you're doing, what kind of training, if any, did you undertake?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: When I started work, we undertook a six-week initial training course to learn the basics of forensic document examination and then undertook a two-year mentoring or tutelage, whereby we gained experience of doing actual case work, and we were taught the basics and the intricacies of doing the work.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And during this training period did you undertake handwriting comparisons already during this time?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: Yes, we undertook them on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Now, what was the institution that you first worked for upon receiving your Ph.D.?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: I joined the Metropolitan Police Forensic Science Laboratory.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And how long did you stay at the metropolitan laboratory?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: Until -- it was taken over by the Forensic Science Service and I worked for that organisation until 1999.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And where did you go in 1999?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: I left to join the company I'm with now, which is Document Evidence Limited.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And what kind of an organisation is this?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: Again, it's a forensic document examination. It's all the work that we do, primarily for police forces within the UK but also civil work, defence work, work for corporations.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And what -- what is the title of your position there?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: I'm a forensic document examiner.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And what exactly does this position entail in your day-to-day work?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: It involves examining documents for, as I said before, handwriting signature comparisons and all the aspects of forensic document examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And would a forensic document examiner have a specialisation among the various tasks you've listed?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: No. Generally, we would say that to be a good forensic document examiner you need to be able to examine all the documents. It's no good being able to examine a signature and then not realise the page it's on has been inserted. So most forensic document examiners specialise in the totality.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: So in the course of your career you yourself have undertake all the task you have listed for us so far?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: I have, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And you have therefore been working on forensic document analysis since 1992?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: I have, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And during these 15 years how many handwriting comparisons have you done would you say?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: I've no idea. Many thousands.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Could you please describe briefly what sort of documents are involved in the comparisons that you do on a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: On a daily basis it can be any type of document. Obviously, fraud is an obvious one, so cheques and credit cards, but also literally any document that has handwriting on it, from anonymous letters, confessions, signatures on mortgage documents, wills, legal documents, anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And, Dr. Barr, have you previously given evidence in court on the basis of your document examination work?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: I have, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Approximately how many times?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: Probably about 50 times.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And you have also given evidence before this Tribunal in the Prosecutor versus Blagojevic case; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: I have, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Now, are there other professional activities you undertake in addition to the work that you do?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: Yes. I do lecturing to other financial organisations, other investigators, training of forensic -- other forensic scientists both in the UK and abroad, and I'm also involved in -- as a supervision of a Ph.D. student, and in research, government-funded research with the university as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Do you have any accreditation as a forensic document examiner?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: Yes. I'm also a member of the Council for the Registration of Forensic Practitioners, which was an organisation set up in the UK to accredit forensic scientists.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to ask you to explain the field of handwriting analysis and comparison and the methodology that's involved in that. Could you please give us a brief definition of what is handwriting?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: Handwriting is basically using character shapes as a representation of language to enable people to communicate.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And are there -- can you describe what the fundamental concepts are in the field of handwriting analysis?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: Generally a handwriting comparison will take three main parts. Initially there will be an analysis of the writing. In that case it's determining actually how the characters have been constructed, so how the pen has moved across the paper to form them. As a part of that you will also look at things like how the characters slant, how they join from one to the other, how fluently they're written.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry to interrupt, but perhaps we -- we can deal with this in the beginning. There is a European organisation set up that brings together forensic experts from all over Europe with a view to fostering exchange of expertise, but also standardising the practices. Do you belong to that organisation? Have you participated in its activities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The company as a whole are associate members of it, and I've been to conferences, and a part of the subgroups of it, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: So you were just mentioning certain terms, including "slant" and how fluently words are written. Could you explain a little bit in more detail what fluency means, what slant is?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: Slant is obviously whether the characters are written in an upwards or whether they slant forwards or backwards. Fluency is indication of the speed with which the writing occurs.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And you began your explanation of the process by saying that there are three main parts to the analysis. You just mentioned that there was construction.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: So you would look at the analysis, you'd work out the construction. You'd also work out the range of variation, because obviously people don't -- they're not robots. Every time they write there will be a variation in their handwriting. But it will only vary within a defined range. You need to be able to assess what that range is. If you were only examining very small amounts of handwriting and you saw differences, you wouldn't be aware of whether they were differences due to two different people or just simply part of a person's natural variation. So basically you work through the alphabet from A to Z, upper case and lower case, and numbers, work out the method of construction, the fluency, and the range of variation. Once you've done that for the writing that's known, you would do exactly the same thing for the questioned writing and then compare the two to determine -- to determine whether there were any similarities or differences. Once that bit's done, then you have to determine whether there are any significance as to those similarities or differences, because obviously within one person's writing or two people's writing there will also be -- there will always be similarities because -- simply by chance because you can't make up your own characters; they have to conform to recognised shapes. Similarly there will always be differences within one person's writing simply by natural variation. So you have to assess whether you consider that the similarities are significant enough to indicate it's one person, or whether the differences indicate that you've got two different writers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And so when you're going through this analysis, you are doing it by going through the individual characters or are you doing it by going through words as a whole?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: Literally going through individual characters.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: So that means you analyse letter by letter?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Is there a specific way you document your analysis, as you proceed through it?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: I use what we would call a tick sheet, which is literally the alphabet written out so just as a means of making sure that you do it in a thorough way, so that you go through literally from A to Z and don't miss characters out.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And does the tick sheet capture the totality of the analysis?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: No. It's part of the analysis. It acts as an aide-memoire and a means of constructing the analysis in a way that not only I can go back to it, but other document examiners could also examine to make sure I followed the direct procedures.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And you produce a tick sheet for both sets of documents, both the specimen and the questioned document?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And once you've gone through both sets of documents, what's the next thing you do? You had mentioned, I believe, the word "range of variation" or the expression. What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: As I say, generally, everybody has a range of variation because they will differ on each occasion that they write but they won't suddenly change -- they don't suddenly change character constructions. They may have different ones in different parts of the word so a character at the middle -- in the middle of a word may be constructed slightly differently from one at the beginning and the end. They're all part of the range of variation of that character.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Can you maybe give us an example of some types of variation, whether it be a similarity or a difference that would be significant at this stage of the analysis?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: Yes. For example, with an upper case E in English, it could be written as an L with two cross strokes or it could be written as a curved character with just a middle stroke, or it could be written as an upside down L with two cross strokes. So within that one character, you have a lot of variation. Similarly, with a simple character like an O or a zero, sometimes some people will write them in a clockwise direction, some people will write them in an anti-clockwise direction.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: After comparing two sets of documents, and after you've undertaken the assessment process that you just explained to us, how do you as a forensic document examiner express your conclusions?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: We express them on a verbal scale because as yet nobody has been able to work out the statistics to be able to come up with a numerical scale so all document examiners use a verbal scale which starts off with conclusive evidence which would indicate either positive or negative, that you could exclude somebody else from being the writer. Then we would have strong evidence that, for example, two people had written a document and it would be unlikely to be anybody else. Where you have weak evidence, obviously you can't exclude the possibility that somebody else could write in a similar way. And then in the middle we have inconclusive, where we are unable to determine whether or not the same -- whether it was written by one or two people.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: So how many levels of opinion are there all together?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: Seven.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And all these seven form a spectrum of whether it is somebody's handwriting or whether it's not?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Is there quality control that a forensic document examiner undertakes at the conclusion of her analysis?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: Yes. All our work is peer reviewed by another scientist to basically check the results, check -- and check the level that you're coming with, that you've answered the questions that have been asked.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Is it necessary to understand the language of a tested handwriting in order to conduct handwriting comparison?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: No. In a sense, we're looking at the how the characters are being constructed rather than what the words say.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: So would the principles and the methodology that you've explained to us before differ in any way when you're doing analysis of handwriting in a foreign language?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: The principles would be the same. The difficulties with the foreign language is you've got to be aware that you are looking at the right character, because obviously some people slur from one character into another. In your native language, you can normally tell what a word is from its context. You lose that when you can't actually read it. So you've got to be careful to ensure that you are examining exactly the same character. The other point is that there are certain -- one of the parts of being a forensic document examiner is being aware of what the significance of similarities and differences are and those can vary from nationality to nationality. So you've got to be aware that certain characters may be more common in certain nationalities than they are in your own language.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And so are there special precautions a document examiner should take, or measures that the document examiner should apply differently in the case of analysing a document in a foreign language?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: In essence, it's taking more care and making sure you, as I say, are comparing like with like, and that you're taking into account that certain characters will be more common, and it probably is best to err on the side of caution.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Dr. Barr, do you understand the language that's referred to as Bosnian/Croatian/Serbian or B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And were you able to compare handwriting in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Is this the first time that you examine handwriting in a language that you do not understand?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: No. Obviously, we see documents from other European languages, French, Dutch, Spanish, German. Obviously, some I have more knowledge of than others, but again, the principle of the document examination is the same for all Latin languages, Roman language characters.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And for these foreign languages, could you say in what context you were doing handwriting analysis, for what kind of cases?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: Again, off the top of my head it would be all kinds of cases. Often, it will be things like drug importation when you're looking at driver logs or delivery of -- of goods into this country.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the Prosecution has requested over the last few years that you conduct a number of handwriting comparisons; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: It is, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And these requests have resulted in five reports; correct?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Now, I notice that you have brought some documents with you today into the courtroom, and if you wouldn't mind identifying them for the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: Yeah. There are five reports that I've produced dated 16th of July, 2003; 22nd of August, 2003; 22nd of January, 2004; 29th of June, 2006; and the 10th of January, 2007.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Just for the record, the 10 January 2007 report is Exhibit number P02844; 29 June 2006 report is P02845; the 16 July 2003 report is P02846; the 22 August 2003 report is P02847; and the final 27 January 2004 report is P02848. Now, in order to produce the -- these reports you were provided with certain documents; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: I was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: What kinds of documents were these in general? What kinds of groupings?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: I was provided with writings that were identified to me as bearing known or specimen writing of certain individuals and then certain documents that we would call questioned, where I was asked if certain people had produced the entries within those documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Now, could you briefly summarise for the Trial Chamber what you were asked to do with respect to the handwriting analysis of Dragan Jokic in the Prosecutor versus Blagojevic case?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: Yes, I was asked if he had written certain entries within the unofficial duty officer's notebook, specifically, entries on the pages 0293-5743 to 0293-5753.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And can you summarise for us your conclusions?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: Yes. I found that from the entries of 0293-5744 down to 5753 that there was strong evidence that he had produced those entries.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And this conclusion -- which report was this conclusion reached in?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: That was my first report, the one dated the 16th of July, 2003.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you also wrote two additional reports concerning the handwriting of the same individual, Mr. Jokic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And those two -- what was the purpose of these two reports?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: The second report was to give a bit more detail behind my conclusions from the first report. In the third report I was provided with specimen handwriting that had been produced recently to see if that would enable me to come to a stronger conclusion. And while it enabled -- it enabled me to confirm my opinion, I wasn't able to change my opinion from strong to conclusive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just a moment so that we clear this up. Page 21, line 20. Yes. "I was asked if he had written certain entries in the unofficial duty officer's" -- is it unofficial or official? Unofficial. And could we have the ERN number of that document, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. It's -- just a moment. I can give you the 65 ter as well as the ERNs. The 65 ter for it is 377 and the range for the whole notebook is 0293-5619 to 0293-5806.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: You're welcome, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Barr you had the opportunity to go through large portions of this unofficial duty officer's notebook; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: Yes it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And can you tell the Trial Chamber, if you recall, what kind of writing implement was predominantly used in this notebook?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: Ball-point pen.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Did you notice, however, in some instances pencil writings?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: Yes. Inasmuch as from my report I excluded the pencil writings from my conclusions regarding Mr. Jokic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And why was that?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: Because they appeared to be written by a different person.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now I'd like to turn with you to the two reports that you've written more recently. We've already referred to these a bit earlier but for the record, again, the report dated 10 January 2007 is P02844, and the report dated 29 June 2006 is P02845, could you briefly describe for the Trial Chamber again what it was that you were asked to do, in other words what the purpose of this report was, or these reports were?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: Again, it was to identify whether the three individuals had written entries within the unofficial duty officer notebook, the official duty officer logbook, the IKM logbook and also two typed reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Could you provide us with individual by individual summary of your conclusion? So perhaps let us begin with your findings concerning the handwritings of Mr. Drago Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: Yes, for Mr. Nikolic, I found that within the official duty officer logbook, that there were various entries that showed many significant similarities to his handwriting and signatures and that there were conclusive evidence that he had written those entries. Do you want me to go through them --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: If you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Soljan, I'm sorry to interrupt you but I'm being confused with the terms "unofficial" and "official".

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Have you dealt with it so far.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: I believe we had dealt with this in the past and we had come to an agreement with the Defence. The -- if it's more helpful, I can -- we have -- we have called the unofficial duty officer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I remember the difference between notebook and logbook, but have we dealt with the issue whether they are official ones or unofficial ones? Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: I'll let Mr. McCloskey --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. These were terms that we had adopted from the Blagojevic case that we had passed on to the expert. So she's using these -- these terms as she had used them before. If we can just for our purposes drop the official or unofficial, then we'll be back to what we have agreed on with the Defence or try to -- it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So now I understand. I take it she's sticking to the instructions she was given at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. We -- we -- that's what we called it at the time and since that time we have dropped those official -- so-called official designations, but she's talking about the notebook and the logbook that we -- that we're used to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Thank you for the clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead, Ms. Soljan.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: So if you could perhaps recap what you were just saying.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: So with the logbook, I found that there were certain entries that showed a number of significant similarities to the writing of Mr. Nikolic, such that there was conclusive evidence that he had produced them. Those were the entries for the 1st of May 1995, 15th of May, 1995, 29th of May, 1995, 10th and 11th of June, 1995, 24th of June, 1995, 7th of July, 1995, and 15th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Can you indicate for us, please, what page of your report --

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: That's on page 8 of my report dated the 29th of June.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And for the record, this is ERN 06064359. Could you summarise the rest of your conclusions, please?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: For the IKM logbook, I was asked to look at entries for July the 11th to the 21st. There are four entries for those dates and I found that there was conclusive evidence that Mr. Nikolic didn't produce any of the entries on those specified dates.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And how about the notebook?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: For the notebook, I found that for the entry for the June the 21st there was conclusive evidence that he didn't produce those entries. Also, he didn't produce the entries for June the 30th or July the 10th. As regards the entries for July the 12th to the 17th, I found that there are entries on July the 15th that show significant similarities to his handwriting such that there's conclusive evidence that he produced those entries and those are the only entries within those dates that he produced.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Were there any other conclusions you reached regarding -- or were there any other questioned documents?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: Yes. I was also shown a two-page typed report which was dated the 26th of July, which had two carbon copies and also a two-page typed report dated the 25th of July, 1995, which had four carbon copies. These documents were typed reports with signatures on them, and I found that there was conclusive evidence that Mr. Nikolic had signed all the reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record, Mr. Josse is now present in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Also for the record, the two reports that Dr. Barr has referred to are 65 ter numbers 345 and 385 and the IKM log is 65 ter 935.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Soljan.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Dr. Barr, could you summarise for the Trial Chamber now your conclusions with respect to the handwriting comparisons concerning the handwriting of Ljubislav Strbac?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: Yes. As regards Mr. Strbac, for the logbook I found that there were a number of entries that showed significant similarities to his signature and handwriting such that there was conclusive evidence that he had written them, and that was the entries for 29th of June, 1995, 17th of July and 18th of July, 1995; 28th of July, 1995, and the 6th of August, 1995. Similarly I was asked, regarding entries for July the 11th to the 21st in the IKM logbook, and again there were significant differences between his writing and those four entries and there was conclusive evidence that he had not produced any of the entries in that logbook. For the notebook, I again found that there was conclusive evidence that he hadn't produced the entries for June the 21st, June the 30th, or July the 10th. For the entries for July the 12th to the 17th, I found that there were significant similarities between entries on July the 17th and his handwriting, and there was conclusive evidence that he'd produced those entries, but also conclusive evidence that he hadn't produced any of the other entries for the period July the 12th to the 17th.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And finally, can you briefly summarise for us your findings from your reports regarding the handwriting of Mr. Milorad Trbic?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: As for Mr. Trbic, I found there were similarities and differences between a group of entries in the notebook but that I was unable to assess the significance of those similarities or differences and the result of my conclusion was inconclusive, by which I mean that I can't determine whether or not he produced those entries.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And can you clarify a little bit for the Trial Chamber why -- what were the difficulties? Why was it not possible to assess the significance?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: There were a number of difficulties. Primarily the specimen writing I was provided with for Mr. Trbic was predominantly in the block capital writing style, whereas most of the entries in the notebooks are in a lowercase style and therefore there was an only limited comparison possible between the two.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And did you see the originals or photocopies of the totality of the documents that you have been reviewing?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: The vast majority of the documents I saw were the original documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And in conducting your examination as a forensic document examiner, do you normally deal with originals?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: We would always ask to see originals if originals exist because you can get more detail of the writing from an original than from a copy.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Barr, could we go perhaps in a little bit more detail through the methodology that you used in conducting your handwriting comparison for this case? Just a general question first. Has your analysis here for these two reports been consistent with the methodology you would normally use to compare handwritings?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: Entirely consistent.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And what did you do in this case to address the problem of comparing handwriting in an unknown language?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: It was a mix, really, of doing some background reading on the characters within the B/C/S language and also I had translations of some of the entries and transliterations of other entries to ensure that I was looking at the right characters within the words. In this case, it also helped because there were a lot of writers, some of them, especially Mr. Jokic, wrote in a scribbled manner, so sometimes it was difficult to determine where one character finished and another ended. But equally, there are other writers within the book who were producing very similar entries, that were much more legible, and so I was able to work out what a lot of the words were from cross-comparison between different entries.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And you were therefore able to work out a range of variations for each character?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And after concluding your analysis and comparing the two sets of handwriting, did you then continue to follow the methodology concerning quality control?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And the colleagues who checked your reports are persons who are experienced in the methodology and in handwriting comparisons; correct?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: Yes. More experienced than me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Soljan and Dr. Barr, we're noticing that the -- some of the interpreters, especially in the B/C/S booth are really having difficulties to try and chase -- to catch up with your speed so slow down a little bit, allow short pauses.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: My apologies to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Now, could I get the usher's assistance to place an exhibit on the ELMO, please? It did not make it into the -- this would be P02850. Dr. Barr, do you see -- if we could place both documents side by side. It's not possible. Then I think ELMO is going to be preferable, please. Dr. Barr, if you could please describe for us what these documents are and we may find a different, a better way to show the whole pages shortly.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: Yes. It was produced for the trial of Mr. Jokic, and it was what -- basically a means of illustrating how I undertook the examination. So on the left-hand side there are selected entries taken from the writing that was in question, and on the right-hand side there are entries from his specimen writing.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And could you please explain to us some of the salient features that you analysed for purposes of handwriting analysis? What I'd like you to do first is maybe discuss your analysis leading to a conclusion that the questioned document and the specimen document match. And I think a good way to do it is if you could grab a red pen, which is right behind the computer screen here and circle the portions or the letters that you're analysing which you're saying to be -- yeah?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Dr. Barr, do you think zooming out would help us understand better what process you're going to go through now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think as it's up on the computer screen, it would be easy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because what we can see at least on the monitor -- yeah, okay. All right. I think we can work with that. Yeah, okay. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: So what I'd like you to do if you would, please, focus on the individual points or letters that you're using as a part of your analysis, circle those on each of the pages that you're looking at and maybe put a number next to it once you've explained to us your analysis, please.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: The purpose of this really is to sort of illustrate the type of examination that -- that we would do. So it's a case, as I say, of looking for similarities and differences within the writing and so some of the similarities that are present between the specimen writing and the questioned would be if you look at the Z of -- of Zvornik, if you mark that one A probably because we've got 1 to 3, you can see that it's written very similarly on the 2 in both specimen and the questioned, with very obvious loops both at the top and the bottom. Similarly, the "G" in the 2 is of the same -- same construction between the 2, written similarly to a 6 with a loop to enable it -- be coming out. Other similar would be, in effect, the whole word on the 2. The nice features of that are the angle, the very narrow "S", the way it joins up to the top of the "T", the "T" to the "A" join, and the "J" within that. And so on, across the two documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Could you give us some examples of instances where letters or features do not match?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: Yep. Obviously there are -- the point of this is illustrating both similarities and the differences. So, for example, the capital A in the specimen tends to be written separate strokes, whereas in the questioned it's written as one stroke, and then the additional stroke for the crossbar. There are also, in the questioned writing, the -- the I dots, so for example, there are much more pronounced than they are in the specimens. So there are features that can't be matched between the two sets of writings, which is why I came to the qualified opinion that there was strong evidence that the two sets of writing were by one person.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Now, when you -- when you do your analysis and you're looking and comparing the ways in which the letters are written, the fluidity or the fluency, the connectivity and so on, when would something be a significant difference as opposed to just a difference that could be accidental?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: Again, I would use my experience to interpret the significance of those differences, but, for example, generally, for example, most people do their -- the I form as a simple down stroke. Consequently it is very easy for that to match simply by chance, whereas more complicated structures it's less obvious that you would get chance matches.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And if one person writes the same text on two different occasions, would that text be identical or would the handwriting be identical?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: No, it wouldn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And why not?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: Because nobody's able to reproduce their handwriting identically from one occasion to another. Simply by a natural variation, there will always be differences within the handwritings of one person.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have no more questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Soljan. Who is going first? Yes. We are going to save so she needs to date it and sign it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: If you could just sign and date it at the bottom of the page?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That can be saved as one document, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sign and date it on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We were going to suggest, Mr. Ostojic, that we have the break now instead of in 15 minutes' time. Right. It will help everyone reorganise a little bit because I asked for all the documentation and what I got was definitely not all the documentation. So we need a break ourselves too. So we'll have a 25-minute break, and we'll start after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I understand you're going first, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could you introduce yourself to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Ma'am, my name is John Ostojic, I represent Ljubisa Beara. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: May I proceed, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'd like to first discuss your qualifications, if I may, with all due respect. I note that your CV -- do you have a copy of your CV with you here?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: Not the most current one, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, I have one of the old ones. You testified today under oath on page 10, lines 24 and 25 that you received a Ph.D. in plant pathology; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Why is that not reflected in your CV?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: Is it not?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't know it was going to be an issue, but I have your CV with ERN number 06055075 through 06055077, which is three pages and it doesn't reflect that you received a doctorate in plant pathology at all.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: Then it's not something that's ever been an issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, you'll agree with me that your qualifications are important in order for someone to judge the amount of weight they should give your testimony as a purported expert, would you not?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, why in your CV do you state that you received a doctorate or Ph.D. in philosophy in 1993?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: Because that's my qualification; it's a Ph.D. I've merely not stated what subject it's in.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me have, with the Court's permission, because I didn't know it was going to be an issue until the witness testified, if she can tender to the witness her curriculum vitae with the ERN numbers and of course, show it to the Prosecution first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: By all means, Mr. Ostojic. Same advisory as before. We have again noticed that the B/C/S booth is having difficulties. You're going a little bit too fast. So please allow a pause between question and answer. This time it's more you than the witness actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, and I'll try to do that. So if Madam Usher would please -- okay. We do have it in e-court. Thank you. If we can enlarge it just briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Is that your CV, Ms. Barr?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: It is, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And who prepared that CV for you?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And when did you prepare it?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: Some time this year.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And can you show me where it says that you received a doctorate or a Ph.D. in plant pathology?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: The qualification is the doctor of philosophy. The subject matter is what's missing from there, but it would be a Ph.D. in whatever subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Is philosophy not a subject?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: The doctorate is a doctorate of philosophy. That's what it's called in the UK in whatever subject it's in.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Is plant pathology a science or an art?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: It's a science.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And the reason you tell us now that you have plant pathology, is it not, because in order to be considered qualified as a forensic document examiner you must have at the very least some sort of degree in a scientific field; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And although your resume doesn't reflect it, you're saying that your scientific field is plant pathology; correct?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: Yes. Well, my original degree, although it states it's a master of arts is actually in a science degree.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And what degree was that?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: Botany.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, you discussed briefly today on page 11 of your transcript other things that a forensic document examiner would do in the course of their normal duties, such as counterfeit documents, typewriting and printer evaluations, indented impressions and alterations of impressions among other things; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, share with me, if you will, more what does it mean when you say "an indented impression"?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: When you write on a piece of paper you get indentations on the sheets below and those are, obviously depending on how much pressure you use to write, those impressions are normally visible on the sheet below but will be present probably up to six sheets below the one that it's actually written on.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Could you determine as a document examiner, ma'am, whether an addition was made on a certain page by looking at the indentations of that particular piece of paper?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: Possibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. But isn't that what indented impressions are, to determine if it was an add-on or a late addition to a various document?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: No, more to determine what was written on a page that was resting. For example, if you have a notepad what was written on the sheet that's missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And how would you determine -- what sources or what tools would you use to determine if something was an indented impression or not?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: We would normally either use an oblique light source or a piece of equipment called Electrostatic Detection Apparatus.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And that's the ESDA?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: It is, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: The same question with the alterations of impressions, how would you detect an alteration of an impression?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: Normally by using specialised lighting equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And that's ultraviolet red lighting?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: Yes, the ultraviolet light or infrared light and using different filters to determine.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: This Electrostatic Detection Apparatus and the infrared video equipment, that's something that's available in your company that you work at today; correct?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And it had been available in your company from the time that you've been there, correct?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you use any of those tools in order to make any assessment as you reflected in your five reports that you shared with us this morning?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did the Prosecutor at any time give you any intercept books to determine whether there were any additions, deletions, modifications or alterations of any intercept books or writers?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you or your company have an agreement with the Office of the Prosecutor that Defence attorneys cannot utilise you without their permission?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: Not that I'm aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the department of forensic -- the Forensic Examiners Institute with the Ministry of Justice here in the Netherlands? Are you familiar with that institution?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: I'm aware of the forensic institutes in the Netherlands.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And do you know if they've worked for the Prosecutor from time to time?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Have you given any reports or offered any consultations with the Prosecution on any other matters on any other matters other than these five reports that you've generated --

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: -- that we've discussed today?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How would you as a forensic document examiner be able to determine if there was an addition to a page by another person if they wanted to add a name or add a section to a specific document? What's the methodology that you would utilise?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: If it was a reasonable amount of handwriting then from the handwriting comparison. If it was, for example, just, say, a stroke changing one character into another, then you could look at the differences in inks.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you utilise any ink comparisons or inter-comparisons of papers or inks while you prepared any of these reports?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: Because it wasn't an issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: According to who?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: I was asked to examine the handwriting and that's what I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, did the Prosecutor orally or verbally advise you of what your task was or was it reduced in writing?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: It was initially in writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you happen to have that initial correspondence?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: May I see it?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: It's in my notes, which I would have to get.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, maybe we can do that later with the Court's permission or indulgence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, perhaps we can go one step further. Are your notes in The Hague or are they in London?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In The Hague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Here in The Hague. Okay. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Is there a way that a forensic document examiner can determine the date or the age of a paper, a piece of paper?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Is there a way that a forensic document examiner can date an ink block or splatter?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can a forensic document examiner determine if there's a difference in the ink that's utilised on a piece of paper?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: If the inks are different, yes, providing they react differently under different light sources, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Different not just by colour but also by the thickness of the pen, for example, or the ink itself?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: It would be the ink itself rather than the thickness.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And what analysis, if any, did you in formulating your reports, did you use to determine if the ink was different that was utilised in, let's say, the duty officer - I want to get the right word here - notebook? Which is I think 377, just for the record.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: I didn't. I think there are from recollection different inks being used in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know if there were different inks being used on the same given day?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: Off the top of my head, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know if there were -- you mentioned pencils in your direct examination. Why didn't you evaluate who or how or when these pencil entries were made for dates?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: As to who, I was asked specifically -- the only specimen or writing I had at that time was Mr. Jokic's writing, so I couldn't evaluate who. As to when they were added, it's not possible to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, but your first three reports were involving Mr. Jokic. Did you not take a specimen or have a specimen to determine if he actually made those entries?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: I excluded them from that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Where is that in your report?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: On page 8, I think, which is when I -- page 3 of my first report.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Oh, the report dated the 16th of July, 2003?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you point it out to me, please?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: Paragraph 5.3. It starts, "I have found similarities between the specimen writing of Dragan Jokic and the following questioned entries for 0293-5744", it says excluding the pencil date and name.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: As well as 5745; correct?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How about any other pencil dates? Did you examine those?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I note on 5753 that you only found his handwriting to be the first four lines; correct?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Immediately underneath that there's another date. Do you know who wrote that date?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you ever learn from the Prosecutor who wrote those dates in?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: Only yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. And that was during what we call your proofing session?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And who advised you of that?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And what did Mr. McCloskey tell you?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: He told me that those had been added after the book had been -- when it was being used, before somebody else had taken the book and added entries to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did he tell you by whom?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did he tell you there were any other changes or additions made to the duty officer notebook?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you ask him?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters kindly ask the speakers to make pauses and slow down. This is highly technical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did you hear that, Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I did, Your Honour, and I'm pausing. I apologise to it the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Dr. Barr.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And just generally, and we'll get to some of the specifics later today, you discussed briefly quality assurance this morning?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: In your report, it doesn't indicate who the person was that purportedly reviewed your work; correct?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now would you agree with me that when we discuss quality assurance that the best practice and the reasonable practice is to have an independent person, forensic document examiner, review the work that you have conducted; correct?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: Independent, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, if you could tell me who the person was that reviewed your work and that agreed with you on the work that you performed.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: It was one of my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: At the same company --

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: -- or a different company?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: At the same company.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, how independent is that?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: As independent as it could be.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How about this as an alternative, that you use some other different forensic document examiner from a different company, in order to evaluate your work. Wouldn't that be just as independent?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: It would but it wouldn't be practical.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And why is that?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: Because it would take too long and nobody would be willing to undertake it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: With whom did you check when you made that determination?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: It's not standard practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar that the Ministry of Justice here in the Netherlands in their forensic department suggest that it should be done by an independent forensic examiner?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of what the European standard is for quality assurance and verifying whether a document examiner's report is actually accurate in order to determine what weight, if any, to give them?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: I'm not aware of the of details of it but I am aware that there is a European standard and as far as I'm aware that is checking with another document examiner, not necessarily one from another company.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Who -- but an independent nonetheless; correct?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: A different document examiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Doesn't have to be independent?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: It depends what you mean by independent.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm just using your word. You have said it's --

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: Independent of me.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down for the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you describe for me, ma'am, what's the difference between peer review checking of each case, and quality assurance by an independent examiner of each case? Would you draw a distinction between the two?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, in any of the five reports did you utilise any tools such as those that we've discussed, the infrared video equipment or the ESDA, which is the Electrostatic - is that right, static - Detection Apparatus?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Who was the person who did your peer review checking of your five reports here?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: There was actually a mix. One was my -- originally my colleague, Dr. Baxendale for the first three reports, and then my colleague Mr. Coslett did it for the -- the two later ones.
