utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Was it more or less than six?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know if it was more or less than 10?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Who would know that information?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: But when you evaluated these 10 pages, did you mark out to say this section or this sentence or this page is not any of the four individuals that the Prosecution asked you --

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That's okay. Do you think it's important in order to give an objective opinion as a handwriting document examiner, given the limited 10 pages with respect to this notebook at the very least, to give us an indication as to the number of different handwritings you observed in this notebook 377?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: For me being objective -- I think for me being objective it makes no difference how many writers there are there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And why is that?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: Because I'm looking at the writers I'm asked to look at. How many others are there as well is immaterial.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: But would it be immaterial if you knew that there were more than 10 different -- or 10 different writings within these 10 different pages for you to be able to determine or make this comparative analysis that you do with like-to-like comparisons?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: Because I'm simply looking at the number of writers. I'm looking at the writings of all the individual ones. So whether there's one extra one or 10 extra ones doesn't really make any difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, staying with this page 5748, I think we have it there, do you see the date that's in the middle of the page there? "13.7.95."

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you just share with it whether that was written in pen or pencil?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: Pen.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know if it was the same pen as the ink generated below it? Meaning the words that follow it and immediately the three lines below that.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Because we didn't do any ink analysis or anything?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: Yes, and you specifically asked if it was the same pen. I could tell you whether it was a different pen. I probably couldn't tell you whether it was the same pen, just because obviously ball-point pens are made in vast numbers and pens from the same box will probably contain the same ink. So if they were different, they would be different. If it was similar, I would say it was a similar ink. I couldn't say it was the same pen.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Does the fact that there's a date written in pen versus a date written in pencil influence or impact your opinion as to whether or not there was additions or modifications made to these 10 pages of the notebook?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: Clearly, if something's -- there are writings in pencil then it indicates that something has been added because it's not all in the same pen. To that extent, yes, but then -- yeah. That's --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I think two pages of on 0293-5745 we have a date on the top left-hand corner which is"14.07."; do you see that?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Is that in pen or pencil?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: Pencil.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Is that significant in any way?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: To what extent?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: To the extent that you're giving an opinion based on handwriting expertise.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: I've excluded it from, I think -- 4, 5. I've excluded it from my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: But isn't it true, Doctor, that you excluded it because the Prosecution asked to exclude it, and you didn't exclude it but they told you that these things were additions with pencil?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What about the page prior to that where it has the date again "14.07." and then the name Jokic?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you exclude that as well?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: I was asked to go from that date.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I understand that. So did you look at that entry at all?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: To a limited extent.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you look at that specific writing, "14.07. Jokic"?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: Not as part of my examination, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: Because I wasn't asked to look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do we know as we sit here whose handwriting that is?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do we know who other than Mr. Jokic would have wrote his name there?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Is the name Jokic in pen or in pencil?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: Pencil.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: As is the date; correct?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So did you look at the entry three lines immediately below this date that we're discussing and the name in pencil, Jokic?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just a couple more questions on this if you don't mind. Doctor, we reviewed briefly your notebook, and I just want to make sure when we talk about peer review and quality assurance, do you understand them to be the same -- the same things?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: I think this would depend on whether -- what you mean them to be by, whether I think they're the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Why don't you help me and tell me --

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I apologise for cutting you off. Tell me what, if you believe there's a difference between peer review and quality assurance, first of all.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: Again it would depend on your definition. Sorry, not trying to be awkward, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: What -- what -- there are quality assurance procedures within the organisation, for example, relating to our management aspect, how we type up the statements, correcting spellings as far as possible and that type of thing. That would be --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: -- quality assurance, which is part of -- of our quality assurance procedures. We also have peer review, which is when your findings are checked by a colleague.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: The quality assurance is -- are sometimes used the ISO 9000; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Then are there any other standards for quality assurance other than for those management systems such as the ISO 9000?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: There are qualities assurance systems in place, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And what are those?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: I know that there is a UK accreditation system that is also in place.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: For document examiners; correct?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: I don't know for certain. As far as I'm aware there are no document examiners qualified to that standard.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: To the extent that you say this logbook, it would take a lot of time to re-evaluate, can you give me a guesstimate to the best of your experience and training as to how long it would take to evaluate the entire notebook that you have before you? Yes.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: For what would be the question, how many writers or whether it's one particular writer?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Both.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: No, not off the top of my head. I'd need to think about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, I know that you've told us you didn't look at any intercept communications that were purportedly reduced to writing, but I'd like to show you one if I may and that would be 65 ter number 1164. If we can have the English version on the e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The document is under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Oh. And I wrote down that I should ask the Court for permission, and I apologise. I didn't check that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's under seal anyway. But it's okay. We can handle that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we are in open session. Mr. Ostojic, Ms. Soljan has questioned the relevance of this part of your testimony. What's your comment to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, I disagree with her, and quite candidly, I think if we relate back - two points, 1, the documents were obviously released to them --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please switch the microphone on. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: The documents were released to them in a timely manner. They've had notice of that. They knew that I was going to use the documents. But more importantly -- more importantly, if we -- they're saying no now, but I know we -- I have indication I released them last night, so I'll check on that. And that was my understanding that they were released to my learned friends. More importantly, if we compare that to the testimony of Stefanie Frease who came to this court in connection with some of these intercepts and the fact that there were unavailability of certain experts purportedly from the OTP, without having a page citation I think it's important at least to draw from this expert, to establish with the changes specifically made to this document, as to what weight she would give, if any, that had various - as we've coined them from time to time - modifications, alterations and changes within the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before we decide -- before we are in a position to decide, Mr. Ostojic, I think it would help us if we knew what your next question will be, your next question to the witness so that we can address the objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It would be as follows: To the extent --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: To the extent that a writer to a certain document would acknowledge that there were changes or modifications to the document, would that strengthen or weaken an opinion if the document was actually authentic or original in its form. And I think the doctor can answer that without even looking at this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's what I was going to say. I mean, I don't think she would need to look at this document, specially if you are proposing to show her the English version thereof, but -- yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. If we're going to my witness, which I believe he is, we're talking about an intercept operator that said he went through and as he listened to the intercept he was, as you know -- I don't need to tell you. You remember. He was hearing things better. That has nothing whatsoever to do with this as I see it. It's apples and oranges. This witness has nothing to do with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we are unanimous on this. We think that this goes beyond the scope of what Dr. Barr is here for, so we suggest that you proceed to your next question instead of focusing on this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor, for your patience. And let me ask you for a general premises: If a document is altered would that -- and it's known to be altered, whether by an initial or by word, would that weaken or strengthen the conclusion that the document is authentic in your view?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: It would depend on a lot of other factors.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Such as what?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: I could give no opinion on whether something was authentic depending on whether it's got alterations or additions to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now what if there was a two-page document, hypothetically --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Soljan.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: My apologies for the interrupt but I believe, page 96, line 2 the witness said I could give no opinion. I guess it just got corrected. My apologies for that. But while I'm still standing up I'd like to make the same objection about the scope of examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think so. Actually, you put the same question again, phrasing it differently when we told you that this is beyond the scope of what Dr. Barr is here for.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I may have misunderstood the Court. I thought we just couldn't use that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Doctor, why couldn't you give an opinion on whether something was authentic or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm following up on her answer, Mr. President, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but it was an answer given to a question that we had indicated shouldn't be put in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you share with us --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I just wanted to make sure the Court was --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you share with us what factors you would look at in order to determine whether or not a document is authentic?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: It would depend on what document it was and what you were meaning by the words "authentic" because authentic can mean is it authentic, somebody's handwriting or is it a genuine document, a passport, a driving licence, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, given that your training and experience is in handwriting, let's limit my question to this question of authenticity to be merely for handwritings. What are the factors that you would look to to determine whether a handwriting was authentic?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: What I said before. You would need samples of a person's known or specimen writing to enable you to compare it with what was in dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Through, Dr. Barr. Your Honour, I don't have any further questions other than those that may be derived from the notebooks or notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. So we'll take that up tomorrow. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I heard you before stating that you would limit your cross-examination to one particular part of her reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, actually, Mr. President, my cross-examination deals with the report that deals with my client but those are practical considerations that I need to clarify from the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Of the expert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Regarding your report, Dr. Barr, dated 29 June 2006, I'd like to refer you to paragraph 6.11 of that report. I take it you have the report with you.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: At paragraph 6.11, you refer to the date of July the 15th, and you also refer to one of the pages that is there, and I refer here to page 0293-5760. And where you say that all the writing, excluding the last two lines fall in a category for which you say there are significant similarities to his handwriting. Now, my first question is: When you did those comparisons concerning the duty officer notebook, of which this page was part of, and I refer now to the title that is just over -- above paragraph 6.8, did you ask for an English translation of those pages to help you out in your analysis?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: I had a translation of some of the documents. I can't remember whether I had the translation of this one in particular.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Actually because my question really is really something of practical consideration but I need to highlight this out so you can confirm with us. And if I can have on e-court please this page, which is the page 5760, and that's in B/C/S. And if I can have that side by side with the English page in the same document, and that's page 23 or ERN 9355. And it's the P377. Sorry for not mentioning that. If I can have this side by side on the e-court. And, Doctor, my question is simply when you produce your expertise and your conclusions in this paragraph 6.11, I take it that your expertise is based solely on the original document that you look at and not a consideration whether the lines match the English translation?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Would that be a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: When I refer to lines, it's from the original document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, the reason I wanted to -- if we can scroll up a bit, the left side. If we get the bottom part of the document. Now, in your report you say that those last two lines of this document are excluded from those for which there was significant similarities; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, if I look on the right side of the of screen, which is the English translation, I would just like you to confirm that those last two lines do not correspond to the last two lines in the English version.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And maybe if we can get somebody to read -- and the only thing I want to bring up to the Court's attention it, Mr. President, is that the last two line actually in the English version actually start where it says, "In the Memici sector," and before that it's not the last two lines. That's what I wanted to confirm. So if we look on the right side, it says, "Died today, duty officer from Zlatar reported." That's not part of the last two lines in the original version. In the original version the last two lines begin with "In the Memici sector."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think the Prosecution could agree to that. I mean, it's -- it's clear from the screen itself. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The translator tried to mirror as best they could this -- to try to avoid this issue. It's not always perfect, but, yeah, we agree that that's -- that's correct, and we're getting an exhibit of this and we'll try to work that out so it's better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Going on from the next page where, again, that's page 10 of your report, but then you refer to the next page 5761 and you say - and if I can have both of these pages up going one page further, both in the B/C/S version on the left and the English version on the right - in this part you say that all of this page falls in a category where there were similarities, but it says "From and including," and I guess the right pronunciation is "Zetjevi" [phoen], or in English "Request." Now, my question to you is: Were you asked by the Prosecution or did you at any time try to see whether the person who wrote above "Request", that's the part that you do not attribute to Mr. Nikolic, and is that -- did that person who write -- who wrote on this page is the same person who wrote the last two lines on the previous page?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: I didn't make that examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And were you ever asked at any point to draw this conclusion?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Going on. I'd like to -- I refer you to paragraph 6.4 of the report. Well, maybe if I would ask you today to do that would be able to do that for us and to tell it us whether the last two lines of page 5760 were written by the same person as -- who wrote on the top of page 5761?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: I can try, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Can we have both of these pages side by side to have 5760 and 5761 side by side all in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Soljan.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, the witness also has the original book at her disposal that she can take a look at.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And I wasn't going to say now. I could do it, but I'd need to --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: What would you need?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: She needs time obviously.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So it's not something that can be done immediately?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It is something that you can come back to us tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Let us move on to paragraph 6.4 of the report which refers to the duty officer logbook, and you were asked to look at the duty officer logbook, and you were asked to look at pages 6603 until 6754. I take it that this is some 150 pages you were asked to look at in the duty officer logbook.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 6.4 you conclude that a number of entries would have significant similarities to the handwriting and signatures of Mr. Nikolic, and then you list those entries and the specific pages on which they are found.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So I'd just like to confirm with you that from all those pages you looked at, those 150 pages or so, that any entry before the 1st of May, 1995, any entry between those dates that you list and any entries after the 15th of July, 1995, do not present any significant similarities to the handwriting of Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If we move to paragraph 6.6 and 6.7 of your report. And this time you are referring to the forward command post duty officer notebook, and the period you were asked to look at was 11 July to 21 July; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And more specifically, you found -- you said that there were four entries or four series of entries. There was 11 July, 12 July, 13 to 15 July, and then 21 July, and that's at paragraph 6.6 of your report.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So I'd just like to confirm that any other entries -- that none of these entries, sorry, were produced by Nikolic. That's your conclusion at paragraph 6.7.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: Yes, that's my conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So did you do any analysis of any other entries outside of these two dates, that is 11 July to 21 July? Did you look in that book anywhere else to find if there was any writing by Mr. Nikolic that maybe you could use as an additional sample?

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: No, because it's not up to me to decide that it was his writing. So I looked at what I was asked to look at.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So this -- those conclusions are drawn on the material that you had in terms of the writing samples that was provided to you.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Last question is concerning your conclusions with Mr. Trbic, and I refer you to paragraph 8.7 of your report. And again paragraph 8.7 refers to all the documents that are listed in paragraph 8.6, which you looked at.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And your conclusion at paragraph 8.7 is that all these documents at paragraph 8.6 are likely to have been written by one person.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: Yes. There's strong evidence they were by one person.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if I look at the words or the phrases that you use with your expertise, that means that you cannot exclude the possibility that more than one person was involved.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you are unable to say whether these entries, and I refer now to paragraph 8.9, I believe, or again 8.8 but later, that you were unable to say whether these entries were indeed produced by Mr. Trbic.

utterances.speaker: KATHRYN JEAN BARR
utterances.text: I was unable to express that opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. That's all I have. Thank you, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I take it there is no one else going to cross-examine this witness, which means we need to adjourn until tomorrow. However, before we do so -- yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, I have another witness, Your Honour, if you want to use the 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah. Then we could start with another witness. Dr. Barr can be escorted. Thank you, madam. We'll reconvene tomorrow and continue with your testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'd just like to return, Mr. President, to the issue on Friday concerning the intercept, the responses we have to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm coming to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Because we only have 15 minutes left. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But you have made your submissions. So -- yes. Last week there were two submissions that were made, one by Mr. McCloskey asking for an adjournment of the case, particularly that we will not have sittings the first two weeks of July, and the other one, a matter which was raised by Mr. Bourgon and supplemented by Mr. Josse plus others, namely as to the extension of the time limit for the filing of the Defence position on -- document on the intercepts following the Prosecution filing. Let's start with the first one. We, of course, fully understand your concerns. They are not only the concerns of the Prosecution but the understanding of this Trial Chamber is that they are also the concerns of the Defence, and we do appreciate that the known factors attached to the -- to joinder motions do present you both with problems, particularly when it comes to organising, planning your witnesses and planning the case in general. At the same time, I'm sure that you appreciate that we also have a role to play, and once I've stated that we do appreciate the predicament that you find or at least you declare you find yourself in, it is -- it becomes incumbent on us to find a proper balance taking into account the possible scenarios, possible circumstances that would arise if joinder is granted or if joinder is not granted. We've given this a lot of thought over the weekend, and that's why we didn't come with a response last Friday. We have given it a lot of thought. We met again this morning to continue discussing, and as things are at the moment, we do not think that it is appropriate to break for a whole entire three weeks immediately prior to the recess, which is planned to start as from the 21st of July in any case. On balance, however, we do concede that a short break is necessary, which would allow the Prosecution, in particular, to reorganise itself and also focusing on the evidence that can be adduced before the recess, summer recess, pending the determination of the joinder motions. We've therefore decided as follows: We will not be sitting on the following days, that is, this coming week, that is from the 2nd to the 6th of July. And then we will not sit on the 13th of July, which I think would also meet the request of three Defence teams who have got something urgent and important to attend to on that day. And we will also not sit on the 16th of July. So we will be sitting the other days, and you, Mr. McCloskey, need to plan of a little bit, I think. This strikes a more or less a -- what we consider to be a reasonable -- more reasonable approach to the problem than stopping for an entire three weeks and then to be followed immediately afterwards by -- by summer recess. We have also given a thought about your submission, Mr. Bourgon, and also the submission by Mr. Josse in particular that it would be more appropriate if the filing of the Defence document on intercepts be delayed until after the joinder motion is determined -- are determined. We have thought about that. We are not in a position, as at the moment, to know when the joinder motions will be decided, and even more so if we will be in a position to decide them before the summer recess, because there are so many imponderables and unknown factors, particularly not knowing what's going to happen in the Tolimir case, which has its additional initial appearance on -- fixed for the 3rd, 3rd of July. We don't know if counsel has been assigned to him. We don't know if he has a position on joinder. We don't know if the problem that was pointed out by the Defence teams in relation to your remuneration, if there is a hiatus, is going to be met with satisfactorily. So there are many questions, and we did not think that delaying the filing of the Defence position on intercepts till after the decision on the joinder motion would be appropriate. So -- we also understand that if you have problems in filing it immediately, that is something that we need to attend to as well and give attention to. So the conclusion we have come to is that we are extending the time limit until the 9th of July. That's Monday, a fortnight from today, which should give you ample time, et cetera. If later on we come to a joinder, which I don't know if we are ever going to come to, but in that case we'll obviously have to discuss what Tolimir's position will be. So that's the position. I hope it meets you halfway, both of you, and that it is satisfactory to -- these arrangements are satisfactory to both of you. We adjourn until tomorrow. Tomorrow we are sitting in the morning, 9.00 a.m. Thank you.
